rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad defines dulūk as the interval from the sun’s decline until sunset; another view makes it sunset itself.
rows.anchor: قال المبرد دلوك الشمس من لدن زوالها إلى غروبها وقيل هو الغروب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dulūk derives from rubbing: observers rub their eyes against the sun’s glare, either at its decline or when discerning it at sunset.
rows.anchor: فسمي الزوال دلوكا لأن الناظر إليها يدلك عينيه لشدة شعاعها

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: Thaʿlab says the sun has tilted when described as dālikat.
rows.anchor: قال ثعلب: دلكت الشمس مالت

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj explains barāḥ as the sun’s decline, when the observer shades the eyes with a palm; he cites a rajaz line about the sun declining while Rabāḥ stands there.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: يقال دلكت براح وبراح أي مالت للزوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With fatḥa, barāḥ is a proper name for the sun on the pattern of Qaṭām and Ḥadhām; with kasra, it means the observer’s palm, as al-Farrāʾ explains.
rows.anchor: ومن قال براح بفتح الباء جعلها اسما للشمس مبنيا على فعال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghasaq denotes the onset or appearance of night’s darkness; the same root describes a bursting sore revealing what is inside.
rows.anchor: وغسق الليل ظهور ظلامه يقال غسقت القرحة إذا انفجرت فظهر ما فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tahajjud is wakefulness and staying up so as to dispel sleep, while hajūd originally means sleep; the author cites Labīd and two other poets using it for sleeping.
rows.anchor: والهجود النوم وهو الأصل هجد يهجد نام وقد هجدته إذا نومته

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad defines tahajjud as staying awake for prayer or remembrance of God.
rows.anchor: قال المبرد التهجد السهر للصلاة أو لذكر الله

rows.speaker: علقمة
rows.claim: ʿAlqama says tahajjud takes place after a person has slept.
rows.anchor: وقال علقمة التهجد يكون بعد نومة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāfila and nafl can mean booty; Labīd’s verse uses nafl for a gift or bounty, while God’s ʿasā conveys certainty and obligation.
rows.anchor: قال لبيد: إن تقوى ربنا خير نفل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A line attributed to Ibn Muqbil uses ʿasā for certainty, supporting the claim that God’s promise is certain.
rows.anchor: وقد أنشد لابن مقبل في وجوبها: ظني بهم كعسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zuhūq means destruction and disappearance: when a soul departs, it is as though destruction has left with it.
rows.anchor: والزهوق الهلاك والبطلان يقال زهقت نفسه إذا خرجت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurʾān al-fajr is accusative by an understood command, aqim; nāfilatan laka is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier.
rows.anchor: قرآن الفجر منصوب على تقدير وأقم قرآن الفجر وانتصب قوله نافلة لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After setting out proofs and warning, God commands the Prophet—and by extension others—to establish prayer from the sun’s decline to nightfall.
rows.anchor: ثم أمر سبحانه بعد إقامة البينات وذكر الوعد والوعيد بإقامة الصلاة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, Jābir, and several Successors take dulūk as the sun’s decline, making the commanded prayer ẓuhr; this is also transmitted from al-Bāqir and al-Ṣādiq.
rows.anchor: وهو قول ابن عباس بخلاف وابن عمر وجابر وأبي العالية والحسن

rows.speaker: النخعي
rows.claim: Al-Nakhaʿī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and al-Suddī take dulūk as sunset, making the prayer maghrib; this is also reported from Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: وهو قول النخعي والضحاك والسدي والصلاة المأمور بها على هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers decline because it lets the passage encompass all five obligatory prayers rather than only one prayer time.
rows.anchor: والقول الأول هو الأوجه لتكون الآية جامعة للصلوات الخمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the preferred reading, decline-time prayers are ẓuhr and ʿaṣr, nightfall prayers are maghrib and later ʿishāʾ, and Qurʾān al-fajr is dawn prayer.
rows.anchor: صلاتا دلوك الشمس الظهر والعصر وصلاتا غسق الليل هما المغرب والعشاء الآخر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda call ghasaq the first onset of night; Mujāhid calls it sunset, al-Jubbāʾī its darkness, and al-Bāqir and al-Ṣādiq midnight.
rows.anchor: وهو أول بدء الليل عن ابن عباس وقتادة وقيل هو غروب الشمس عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: بعض أصحابنا
rows.claim: Some companions infer that ẓuhr’s time extends to the end of the day because the verse makes the interval from decline to nightfall a prayer time.
rows.anchor: واستدل قوم من أصحابنا بالآية على أن وقت صلاة الظهر موسع إلى آخر النهار

rows.speaker: الشيخ أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Shaykh Abū Jaʿfar rejects that inference: sunset concerns maghrib until twilight, while decline may summarize all five prayers rather than one prayer’s time.
rows.anchor: ولم يرتضه الشيخ أبو جعفر قدس الله روحه قال: لأن من قال إن الدلوك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author answers that decline to nightfall can be shared time for four prayers: ẓuhr and ʿaṣr share decline-to-sunset, and maghrib and ʿishāʾ share sunset-to-nightfall.
rows.anchor: جعل من دلوك الشمس الذي هو الزوال إلى غسق الليل وقتا للصلوات الأربع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse establishes the obligation and timing of five prayers, singling out dawn prayer as Qurʾān al-fajr.
rows.anchor: ففي الآية بيان وجوب الصلوات الخمس وبيان أوقاتها

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Al-ʿAyyāshī transmits from ʿUbayd b. Zurāra that Abū ʿAbd Allāh assigns two prayers from decline to sunset and two from sunset to midnight, ordered within each pair.
rows.anchor: عن عبيد بن زرارة عن أبي عبد الله ع وفي هذه الآية قال

rows.speaker: المرتضى
rows.claim: Al-Murtaḍā adopts this account of the prayer times.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا ذهب المرتضى علم الهدى قدس روحه في أوقات الصلوات

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says the separate mention of Qurʾān al-fajr shows prayer must include recitation.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: إن في قوله وقرآن الفجر فائدة عظيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All commentators say dawn prayer is witnessed by angels of night and day; the Prophet’s congregational-prayer report is cited from al-Bukhārī’s Ṣaḥīḥ.
rows.anchor: كلهم قالوا معناه أن صلاة الفجر تشهدها ملائكة الليل وملائكة النهار

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet says congregational prayer is twenty-five times superior to individual prayer and night and day angels assemble for dawn prayer; al-Bukhārī includes it in his Ṣaḥīḥ.
rows.anchor: تفضل صلاة الجماعة صلاة أحدكم وحده بخمسة وعشرين جزءا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains tahajjud with the Qurʾān as praying at night by reciting it.
rows.anchor: أي فصل بالقرآن عن ابن عباس ولا يكون التهجد إلا بعد النوم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid, al-Aswad, ʿAlqama, and most exegetes say tahajjud occurs only after sleep.
rows.anchor: ولا يكون التهجد إلا بعد النوم عن مجاهد والأسود وعلقمة وأكثر المفسرين

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Another view calls any voluntary night worship tahajjud, because a mutahajjid casts sleep off himself.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم ما تنفلت به في كل الليل يسمى تهجدا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One interpretation makes night prayer an obligation unique to the Prophet and a voluntary virtue for others.
rows.anchor: أن صلاة الليل كانت فريضة على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم مكتوبة عليه

rows.speaker: قول غير مسمى
rows.claim: Another view says night prayer was first obligatory for the Prophet and this verse later abrogated its obligation.
rows.anchor: وقيل كانت واجبة عليه فنسخ وجوبها بهذه الآية

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: A further interpretation makes night prayer a virtue for the Prophet and expiation for others; Mujāhid adds that the Prophet needs no expiation.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن معناه فضيلة لك وكفارة لغيرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address may include the Prophet and others: he is singled out to invite emulation and following his Sunna; Mujāhid says the Prophet himself needs no expiation.
rows.anchor: وإنما اختصه بالخطاب لما في ذلك من دعاء الغير إلى الاقتداء به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s ʿasā is certain; maqām can mean the act of raising, so the Prophet is raised to a praiseworthy resurrection on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: عسى من الله واجبة والمقام بمعنى البعث فهو مصدر من غير جنسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, raising means establishing him in an honored station where all generations praise him; this is the station of intercession.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يجعل البعث بمعنى الإقامة كما يقال بعثت بعيري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes agree the praised station is intercession, where the Prophet is first to intercede and be granted intercession, and receives the Banner of Praise beneath which prophets and angels gather.
rows.anchor: وقد أجمع المفسرون على أن المقام المحمود هو مقام الشفاعة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid reads entry and departure in truth as asking support to fulfill revelation and the prophetic mission safely.
rows.anchor: أي أعني على الوحي والرسالة عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and Saʿīd b. Jubayr read it as the Prophet’s entry into Medina and departure for the conquest of Mecca.
rows.anchor: أدخلني المدينة وأخرجني منها إلى مكة للفتح عن أبي عباس

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim takes it as a prayer for every undertaking the Prophet enters or leaves to have a truthful and praiseworthy outcome.
rows.anchor: أمر بهذا الدعاء إذا دخل في أمر أو خرج من أمر

rows.speaker: عطية
rows.claim: A report from ʿAṭiyya from Ibn ʿAbbās interprets entry as entering the grave at death and exit as resurrection.
rows.anchor: أدخلني القبر عند الموت مدخل صدق وأخرجني منه عند البعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A truthful entry has an outcome praised in worldly and religious life; attributing entry and exit to God asks for grace bringing the servant nearer to good.
rows.anchor: ومدخل الصدق ما تحمد عاقبته في الدنيا والدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supportive authority means honor and strength to resist those obstructing God’s obligations; another view is a mighty kingdom that makes enemies fear the Prophet a month’s journey away.
rows.anchor: أي اجعل لي عزا امتنع به ممن يحاول صدي عن إقامة فرائضك

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid interprets it as clear proof to prevail over false religions; it is supportive because it brings victory over enemies.
rows.anchor: حجة بينة أتقوى بها على سائر الأديان الباطلة عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The truth appears as Islam and religion.
rows.anchor: أي ظهر الحق وهو الإسلام والدين

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī identifies falsehood as associating partners with God.
rows.anchor: وهو الشرك عن السدي وقيل الحق التوحيد

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil identifies truth with divine unity and worship, and falsehood with idol worship.
rows.anchor: وقيل الحق التوحيد وعبادة الله والباطل عبادة الأصنام عن مقاتل

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda identifies the truth as the Qurʾān and falsehood as Satan; zuhūq means to perish and vanish.
rows.anchor: وقيل الحق القرآن والباطل الشيطان وزهق بطل واضمحل عن قتادة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reports that on entering Mecca the Prophet found 360 idols around the Kaʿba and prodded them while reciting the verse; al-Bukhārī includes the report in his Ṣaḥīḥ.
rows.anchor: وروي عن عبد الله بن مسعود أنه قال دخل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse recited by the Prophet at the idols’ fall is cited from al-Bukhārī’s Ṣaḥīḥ.
rows.anchor: جاء الحق وزهق الباطل إن الباطل كان زهوقا

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī adds that each idol toppled face-first as the Prophet recited, while Meccans called him the most skilled sorcerer they had seen.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي فجعل الصنم ينكب لوجهه إذ قال ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Falsehood is doomed to vanish, perish, and lack stability.
rows.anchor: أي مضمحلا ذاهبا هالكا لا ثبات له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings of naʾā vary: Abū Jaʿfar and Ibn ʿĀmir via Ibn Dhakwān lengthen and hamzate it; some transmitters use naʾi with a fatḥa then kasra, Ḥamza via al-ʿAjalī, Khalaf, and al-Kisāʾī use kasra on both, and the rest read naʾā.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر وابن عامر برواية ابن ذكوان وناء بجانبه ممدودة مهموزة

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī analyzes nāʾ as an inverted fāʿil form and cites a poem using rāʾanī as evidence.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي ناء مثل فاع وهو على القلب وتقديره فلع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imāla follows because the alif derives from yāʾ in naʾy; readers may incline the first vowel toward the second, while others leave it open.
rows.anchor: ومن أمال الفتحتين فلأن الألف منقلبة من الياء التي في النأي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shākila means a path or way; Arabs describe a branching road as one with multiple shākilas.
rows.anchor: الشاكلة الطريق والمذهب يقال هذا طريق ذو شواكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān heals by removing ignorance, doubt, and spiritual blindness through explanation; its miraculous eloquence demonstrates the Prophet’s truthfulness.
rows.anchor: منها ما فيه من البيان الذي يزيل عمى الجهل وحيرة الشك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its recitation brings blessing and helps repel illness and harm as divine wisdom permits; teachings on unity, justice, law, parables, and wisdom benefit people.
rows.anchor: ومنها ما فيه من أدلة التوحيد والعدل وبيان الشرائع والأمثال والحكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurʾānic worship and recitation benefit people in this life and the next; believers receive its mercy because they benefit from it.
rows.anchor: فهو شفاء للناس في دنياهم وآخرتهم ورحمة للمؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wrongdoers lose reward and incur punishment because they disbelieve in the Qurʾān and fail to reflect on it.
rows.anchor: يخسرون الثواب ويستحقون العقاب لكفرهم به وتركهم التدبر له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that supplication only drove them farther away echoes Noah 71:6; alternatively, the Qurʾān exposes their hidden malice and plots against the Prophet.
rows.anchor: فلم يزدهم دعائي إلا فرارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When granted blessings, a person turns from remembrance as if never to have prayed, then distances himself from gratitude and the duties owed for the blessing.
rows.anchor: أي ولى كأنه لم يقبل علينا بالدعاء والابتهال

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid reads distancing himself as turning away from God, implying arrogance, self-exaltation, and conceit.
rows.anchor: معناه تباعد منا وعلى هذا فيكون معناه تجبر وتكبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When hardship, poverty, or affliction strikes, the person despairs instead of patiently hoping for relief, unlike a believer who hopes for relief and mercy.
rows.anchor: وإذا أصابه المحنة والشدة والفقر لم يصبر وكان قنوطا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although phrased generally, the description specifically concerns unbelievers, who expect no reward for illness and recoil from it; afflictions are truly wise and right.
rows.anchor: فيكون المراد بالآية خاصا وإن كان اللفظ عاما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says each person acts according to the nature and disposition with which he was created.
rows.anchor: على طبيعته وخليقته التي تخلق بها عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الفراء والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj interpret shākila as one’s accustomed path and practice.
rows.anchor: وقيل على طريقته وسنته التي اعتادها عن الفراء والزجاج

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī says each acts according to what seems most suited to rightness and truth; God knows which party is rightly guided or astray.
rows.anchor: على ما هو أشكل بالصواب وأولى بالحق عنده عن الجبائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing phrase can mean that God knows best who follows the soundest religion and finest way.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه أنه أعلم بمن هو أصوب دينا وأحسن طريقا

rows.speaker: بعض أرباب اللسان
rows.claim: Some linguists call this the Qurʾān’s most hope-giving verse because divine generosity makes forgiveness fitting for servants.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية أرجى آية في كتاب الله لأن الأليق بكرمه سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ẓahīr means helper, as if allies strengthen one another back-to-back; taṣrīf turns things through directions and speech through different meanings.
rows.anchor: الظهير المعين وهو المظاهر وأصله من الظهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In verse 87, mercy is an exception from the preceding statement: God preserved revelation in the Prophet’s heart; the oath’s answer governs yaʾtūn.
rows.anchor: إلا رحمة من ربك الرحمة استثناء من الأول والمعنى ولكن الله تعالى رحمك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in la-in signals an oath, with the implied sense by God they would never produce its like; Kathīr’s verse illustrates the construction.
rows.anchor: واللام في لئن موطئة للقسم دالة عليه والتقدير فوالله لا يأتون

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī favors the view that they asked about the human spirit; the Prophet withheld an answer because they were obstinate and an answer would deepen their defiance.
rows.anchor: واختاره الجبائي وعلى هذا فإنما عدل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن جوابهم

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, and others say they asked what the spirit in a human body is.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود وابن عباس وجماعة واختاره الجبائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reported Jewish strategy told Quraysh to ask about the spirit as a test: answering would disprove prophethood, while silence would confirm it from their scripture.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل إن اليهود قالت لكفار قريش سلوا محمدا عن الروح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says they asked whether the spirit was created; the answer that it is from God’s command means it is His act and creation.
rows.anchor: أنهم سألوا عن الروح أهي مخلوقة محدثة أم ليست كذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The spirit may be the animating soul, as Ibn ʿAbbās says; alternatives are Gabriel, a vast many-faced angel in a report from ʿAlī, or Jesus, also called spirit.
rows.anchor: فيجوز أن يكون الروح الذي سألوه عنه هو الذي به قوام الجسد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third interpretation takes spirit as the Qurʾān and asks how the angel conveyed it or how its arrangement differs from human speech; God elsewhere calls the Qurʾān a spirit.
rows.anchor: أن المشركين سألوه عن الروح الذي هو القرآن كيف يلقاك به الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the Qurʾān interpretation, revelation is God’s act and proof of prophethood, beyond created beings’ capacity; on the human-spirit view, it means knowledge God withheld.
rows.anchor: إن الروح الذي هو القرآن من أمر ربي أنزله دلالة على دلالة نبوتي

rows.speaker: أكثر المتكلمين
rows.claim: Most theologians, with al-Murtaḍā’s preference, define spirit as a subtle airy body moving through an animal’s passages.
rows.anchor: فقيل إنه جسم رقيق هوائي متردد في مخارق الحيوان

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: ʿAlī b. ʿĪsā calls it an airy body shaped as an animal, with life in every part; animals have body and spirit, though one may predominate.
rows.anchor: عن علي بن عيسى قال فلكل حيوان روح وبدن

rows.speaker: المفيد والبلخي
rows.claim: Al-Mufīd, al-Balkhī, and Baghdadi Muʿtazilites regard spirit as an accident: life enabling a subject to possess power, knowledge, and choice.
rows.anchor: وهو مذهب الشيخ المفيد أبي عبد الله محمد بن محمد بن النعمان والبلخي

rows.speaker: الأسواري
rows.claim: Al-Aswārī says spirit is a meaning located in the heart.
rows.anchor: وقيل هو معنى في القلب عن الأسواري

rows.speaker: ابن الإخشيد والنظام
rows.claim: Ibn al-Ikhshīd and al-Naẓẓām identify spirit with the human being, the living morally responsible person.
rows.anchor: عن ابن الإخشيد والنظام وقال بعض العلماء إن الله تعالى خلق الروح

rows.speaker: بعض العلماء
rows.claim: Some scholars say God created spirit from light, purity, permanence, life, knowledge, and elevation; martyrs remain alive with God after bodily decay.
rows.anchor: إن الله تعالى خلق الروح من ستة أشياء من جوهر النور والطيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading takes limited knowledge to address the Prophet and everyone else: only a little is explicitly disclosed, while God’s knowledge has no end.
rows.anchor: قيل هو خطاب للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وغيره إذا لم يبين له الروح

rows.speaker: اليهود
rows.claim: Another reading addresses the Jews who asked, and they objected that God had given them the Torah, so how could their knowledge be little?
rows.anchor: وقيل خطاب لليهود الذين سألوه فقالت له اليهود عند ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God could remove the Qurʾān He revealed but, through mercy, gave the Prophet what he needed and withheld details he did not need, even if people mistakenly thought them necessary.
rows.anchor: يعني القرآن ومعناه أني أقدر أن آخذ ما أعطيتك كما منعت غيرك

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبو مسلم والأصم
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, Abū Muslim, and al-Aṣamm say God could erase the Qurʾān from the Prophet’s and community’s memories, leaving no trace or keeper.
rows.anchor: حتى لا يوجد له أثر ثم لا تجد له حفيظا يحفظه عليك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The erasure interpretation is evidence that the question about spirit concerned the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: عن الحسن وأبي مسلم والأصم قالوا وفي هذا دلالة على أن السؤال وقع عن القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception means God’s mercy gave the Prophet knowledge, withheld other matters, and established the Qurʾān in his and believers’ hearts; this immense favor calls for gratitude.
rows.anchor: لكن رحمة من الله ربك لك أعطاك ما أعطاك من العلوم ومنعك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains God’s great favor as making the Prophet leader of humanity, seal of prophets, and recipient of the praised station.
rows.anchor: حيث جعلك سيد ولد آدم وختم ربك النبيين وأعطاك المقام المحمود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge covers the Qurʾān’s supreme eloquence, arrangement, meanings, refined expression, and freedom from contradiction or objectionable wording; human and jinn cooperation cannot match it.
rows.anchor: في فصاحته وبلاغته ونظمه على الوجوه التي هو عليها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās compares their failure to poets cooperating to perfect a single verse of poetry.
rows.anchor: مثل ما يتعاون الشعراء على بيت شعر فيقيمونه عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge refutes al-Naḍr b. al-Ḥārith’s boast that his group could produce the same.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا تكذيب للنضر بن الحارث حين قال لو نشاء لقلنا مثل هذا

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim also sees evidence that the question about spirit concerned the Qurʾān, since the challenge follows that discussion.
rows.anchor: قال أبو مسلم: وفي هذا أيضا دلالة على أن السؤال بالروح وقع عن القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God varied examples of every needed proof, lesson, ruling, and religious or worldly matter, yet most people insist on denial; mathal can mean a thing, its description, or likeness.
rows.anchor: لقد بينا لهم في هذا القرآن من كل ما يحتاج إليه من الدلائل والأمثال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kūfan readers and Yaʿqūb read tafjura in a light form; the rest double the jīm, intensifying the spring’s repeated gush though it is singular.
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل الكوفة ويعقوب حتى تفجر لنا بفتح التاء وضم الجيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the requested spring is singular, the light reading fits it; all readers use the intensive form for rivers, as with repeated closing of doors.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ تفجر فلأن الينبوع واحد فلا يكون كقوله فتفجر الأنهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar and Ibn ʿĀmir read kasfan with fatḥa here; Ḥafṣ uses fatḥa except al-Ṭūr, while Iraqi readers and Ibn Kathīr generally use sukūn with exceptions.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر وابن عامر كسفا بفتح السين ها هنا وفي القرآن

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abū Zayd says kasafa al-thawb means to cut a garment into pieces; kasaf can therefore name cut material.
rows.anchor: قال أبو زيد: كسفت الثوب أكسفه كسفا إذا قطعته

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī explains kasfan as the sky falling in pieces; since asqaṭa takes one object, kasfan is a circumstantial accusative describing the sky.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: إذا كان المصدر الكسف فالكسف الشيء المقطوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar and Ibn ʿĀmir read rabbī as the Prophet’s response, while others read the imperative qul, God’s command to answer.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ قال سبحان ربي فالوجه فيه أن الرسول قال عند اقتراحهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tafjīr is splitting open what lets water or light flow; yanbūʿ is where water springs forth, and qabīl can mean guarantor or surety.
rows.anchor: اللغة: التفجير التشقيق عما يجري من ماء أو ضياء

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj allows qabīlan to mean appearing face-to-face so angels may be seen directly; an anonymous poet uses it for one facing another.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج وجائز أن يكون المعنى تأتي بهم حتى نراهم مقابلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zukhruf means ornamentation; a gold house is the fullest example, and the source distinguishes climbing from incantation by vowel pattern.
rows.anchor: وأصل الزخرف من الزخرفة وهي الزينة وزخرفت الشيء إذا أكملت زينته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās recounts that Quraysh leaders offered Muḥammad wealth, leadership, or medical help, then demanded springs, gardens, resurrected ancestors, an angel, treasures, the sky’s fall, God and angels appearing, and ascent with a written message; his refusal led to rejection and Abū Jahl’s threat.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس إن جماعة من قريش وهم عتبة وشيبة ابنا ربيعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the Qurʾān’s inimitability, the passage shows unbelievers persisting in transgression and demanding signs beyond their authority to stipulate.
rows.anchor: لما بين سبحانه فيما تقدم إعجاز القرآن عقب ذلك البيان بأنهم أبوا الكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They demand a spring from Mecca’s relatively water-poor ground before believing Muḥammad’s claim to prophethood.
rows.anchor: أي تشقق لنا من أرض مكة فإنها قليلة الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They also demand a garden of palms and grapevines with rivers split through it, running beneath the trees.
rows.anchor: أي تشقيقا حتى يجري الماء تحت الأشجار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Qatāda understand sky fragments as pieces stacked atop one another; the threat recalls a warning about the sky splitting or Muḥammad’s claim to prophethood.
rows.anchor: أي قطعا قد تركب بعضها على بعض عن ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk take the angels’ coming as guarantors who warrant Muḥammad’s claim.
rows.anchor: أي كفيلا ومعناه تأتي بكل واحدة حتى يكون كفيلا ضامنا لنا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid reads qabīlan as groups of angels arriving one tribe after another.
rows.anchor: وقيل هو جمع القبيلة أي تأتي بأصناف الملائكة قبيلة قبيلة عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: الجبائي وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī and Qatāda take angels as appearing face-to-face to witness the Prophet’s truth; this demand shows polytheists anthropomorphized God alongside idolatry.
rows.anchor: حتى نشاهدهم قبيلا أي مقابلة نعاينهم ويشهدون بأنك حق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Qatāda say the decorated house is gold; al-Ḥasan instead takes zukhruf as ornamentation or engravings.
rows.anchor: أي من ذهب عن ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة وقيل الزخرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They insist they would still disbelieve after ascent unless each received a divine letter, paralleling the demand for distributed pages in 74:52.
rows.anchor: بل يريد كل امرء منهم أن يؤتى صحفا منشرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Subḥāna rabbī declares God above faults; signs are God’s decision according to wisdom, not something the Prophet supplies on demand.
rows.anchor: وفي ذلك من الجواب أنكم تتخيرون الآيات وهي إلى الله سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations say the phrase exalts God beyond servants ruling Him, answers those imagining God as a body, or rejects miracles in response to arbitrary demands.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه تعظيما له عن أن يحكم عليه عبيده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A human messenger cannot personally produce such signs; God grants miracles as wisdom requires, as He did for earlier messengers.
rows.anchor: ليس في طاقة البشر أن يأتي بها وأن يفعلها فلا أقدر بنفسي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that God would not send a human messenger expresses the polytheists’ mistaken distinction between God and worshippers, leading them to direct worship toward idols.
rows.anchor: دخلت عليهم الشبهة في أنه لا يجوز أن يبعث الله رسولا إلا من الملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here prevent is emphatic figurative language for turning people away: actual compulsion would make contrary action impossible and is not intended.
rows.anchor: وإلا فالمنع يستحيل معه الفعل فلا يجوز أن يكون مرادا هنا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan understands hypothetical angels as inhabitants settled on earth; God would send them an angel messenger of their kind.
rows.anchor: رسولا } منهم عن الحسن وقيل معناه مطمئنين

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī says settled means at ease with worldly pleasures, free of fear and religious duties.
rows.anchor: مطمئنين إلى الدنيا ولذاتها غير خائفين ولا متعبدين بشرع

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim says if earth’s inhabitants were angels, an angel would be sent because they understand one of their kind more readily.
rows.anchor: عن أبي مسلم وقيل إن العرب قالوا كنا ساكنين مطمئنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even contented inhabitants need messengers; humans need revelation at least as much as angels, so settled circumstances do not justify rejecting a human prophet.
rows.anchor: فكذلك كون الناس مطمئنين لا يمنع من إرسال الرسول إليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A question asks why a prophet may receive an angel despite differing in kind from his people; prophetic selection and miracles make his state approximate the angels’.
rows.anchor: قالوا إذا جاز أن يكون الرسول إلى النبي ملكا ليس من جنسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ordinary people cannot normally see angels as they see one another; a prophet needs a miracle to recognize his commission, and God makes seeing the angel that miracle.
rows.anchor: لأنه يجوز أن يرى الملائكة كما يرى بعضهم بعضا بخلاف الأمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khubūʾ is a fire’s subsiding; qatūr means restrictive or miserly, an intensive form from qatr, with related verbs meaning to stint spending.
rows.anchor: اللغة: الخبو سكون النار عن الإلتهاب يقال خبت النار تخبو

rows.speaker: عدي بن زيد
rows.claim: ʿAdī b. Zayd’s verse uses khabā for a lamp’s alternation between dimming and shining.
rows.anchor: وسطه كاليراع أو سرج المج دل حينا يخبو وحينا ينير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kafā billāh omits its object, with the bāʾ extra and shahīdan as specification; conditional pronouns follow singular form before plural meaning resumes.
rows.anchor: كفى بالله المفعول محذوف وهو الكاف والباء زيادة وشهيدا تمييز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about hell subsiding can be circumstantial because hell stands for blazing and burning; alternatively it has no syntactic position and an understood conjunction precedes it.
rows.anchor: الجملة في موضع الحال من جهنم لأن جهنم توضع موضع متلظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being dragged on faces is a circumstantial accusative, meaning they are dragged face-down.
rows.anchor: على وجوههم في موضع نصب على الحال وتقديره مجرورين على وجوههم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In law antum tamlikūn, the raised pronoun is explained by an understood verb because law requires a verb, as illustrated by a poetic line.
rows.anchor: أنتم مرفوع بفعل مضمر يفسره هذا الظاهر الذي هو قوله تملكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s testimony confirms the Prophet’s mission; God knows all their states, reinforcing the warning.
rows.anchor: لا يخفى عليه من أحوالهم شيء والمراد به تأكيد الوعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those whom God judges guided are truly guided through sincere obedience; those judged astray have no protector able to remove misguidance.
rows.anchor: أي من يحكم الله بهداه فهو المهتدي بإخلاصه وطاعته على الحقيقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They are dragged to the Fire on their faces as a worldly person might be dragged in extreme humiliation and torment.
rows.anchor: يسحبون على وجوههم إلى النار كما يفعل في الدنيا بمن يبالغ في إهانته

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet answered that the One who made an unbeliever walk on his feet in this world can make him walk on his face on Judgment Day; al-Bukhārī and Muslim include it in their Ṣaḥīḥ collections.
rows.anchor: إن الذي أمشاه على رجليه في الدنيا قادر على أن يمشيه على وجهه يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One interpretation says they are blind to what benefits them, mute about what benefits them, and deaf to what gives them pleasure.
rows.anchor: عميا عما يسرهم بكما عن التكلم بما ينفعهم صما عما يمتعهم

rows.speaker: قول غير مسمى
rows.claim: Another view treats sensory loss as fitting punishment: blind for rejecting truth, mute for refusing confession of divine unity, and deaf for turning from truth to falsehood.
rows.anchor: عميا كما عموا عن الحق في دار الدنيا بكما جزاء على سكوتهم

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil places this state when they are told to be gone in hell and not speak, citing 23:108.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل هذا حين يقال لهم اخسئوا فيها ولا تكلمون

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says they are first gathered blind, mute, and deaf, then given sight, hearing, and speech.
rows.anchor: وقيل يحشرون كذلك ثم يجعلون يبصرون ويسمعون وينطقون عن الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whenever hell’s flames subside, God rekindles them; when asked how the condemned stay alive, He can keep the fire from reaching their vital organs.
rows.anchor: إن الله تعالى قادر على أن يمنع وصول النار إلى مقاتلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their punishment follows disbelief in God’s signs and mockery of resurrection from scattered, pulverized bones.
rows.anchor: أئذا كنا عظاما ورفاتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creating the heavens and earth proves God can create their counterparts and resurrect them, since re-creation is easier than initial creation in familiar experience.
rows.anchor: وإذا كان قادرا على خلق أمثالهم كان قادرا على إعادتهم إذ الإعادة أهون

rows.speaker: قول غير مسمى
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes mithlahum as the people themselves: a thing’s equal can be called the thing, as in “one like you” and 42:11.
rows.anchor: وقيل أراد قادر على أن يخلقهم ثانيا وأراد بمثلهم إياهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God appointed an unquestionable time for their return; alternatively it is a period to reflect or a lifespan ending in death.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه وضرب لهم مدة ليتفكروا ويعلموا فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument implies whoever can create a kind with counterparts can create its opposite and restore what perishes.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية دلالة على أن القادر على الشيء يجب أن يكون قادرا على جنس مثله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s treasures are His possible acts and gifts, not a physical storehouse; if humans owned them, they would hoard from fear of poverty.
rows.anchor: أي ما يقدر عليه ربي من النعم إذ لا يكون له سبحانه موضع يخزن فيه الرحمة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda explain withholding as miserliness from fear of poverty and need.
rows.anchor: خشية الفقر والفاقة عن ابن عباس وقتادة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says they fear that spending itself will leave them poor.
rows.anchor: وقيل خشية أن تنفقوا فتفتقروا عن السدي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda call qatūr miserly; although generous people exist, wording reflects the majority or compares human giving with God’s boundless generosity.
rows.anchor: وظاهر قوله وكان الإنسان قتورا العموم وقد علمنا أن في الناس الجواد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gives abundantly to obedient and disobedient alike without need, unlike humans who give only what exceeds their needs; this answers the earlier demand for a spring.
rows.anchor: وهذا جواب لقولهم لن نؤمن لك حتى تفجر لنا من الأرض ينبوعا

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī alone reads ʿalimta with second-person fatḥa, making Moses tell Pharaoh he knows the signs’ truth; others read first-person ʿalimtu.
rows.anchor: قرأ الكسائي وحده لقد علمت بضم التاء والباقون بفتحها

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī argues for the majority’s first-person reading from Pharaoh’s followers’ promise to believe if affliction were lifted (7:134) and their inward certainty despite denial.
rows.anchor: حجة من فتح أن فرعون ومن كان يتبعه قد علموا صحة أمر موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second-person reading answers the charge that a madman cannot know: Moses asserts sound knowledge rather than sorcery; this reading is attributed to ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib.
rows.anchor: وزعموا أن هذه القراءة رويت عن أمير المؤمنين علي بن أبي طالب ع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thubūr means destruction; mathbūr may mean held back from good, while the verb can mean turning someone away or preventing him.
rows.anchor: الثبور الهلاك ثبره الله يثبره لغتان ورجل مثبور محبوس عن الخيرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lafīf is a verbal noun meaning gathered together; al-Zajjāj calls it groups from different tribes.
rows.anchor: ولفيف مصدر قولك لففت الشيء اي جمعته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk list the nine signs as Moses’s hand, staff, tongue, sea, flood, locusts, lice, frogs, and blood.
rows.anchor: والدم عن ابن عباس والضحاك وقيل الطوفان والجراد

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب
rows.claim: Muḥammad b. Kaʿb lists the plagues, sea, staff, obliteration, and stone; Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī replaces obliteration with the hand.
rows.anchor: عن محمد بن كعب وعن أبي علي الجبائي أيضا إلا أنه ذكر بدل الطمسة اليد

rows.speaker: قتادة وعكرمة وعطاء
rows.claim: Qatāda, ʿIkrima, and ʿAṭāʾ instead include the hand, years of famine, and reduced crops in place of the sea, obliteration, and stone.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة وعكرمة وعطاء كذلك إلا إنهم ذكروا بدل البحر والطمسة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan counts famine and crop loss as one sign and names the staff swallowing the magicians’ fabrications as the ninth.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن مثل ذلك إلا إنه جعل الأخذ بالسنين ونقص من الثمرات

rows.speaker: قول غير مسمى
rows.claim: Another view says the nine signs were legal commandments.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنها تسع آيات في الأحكام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report begins with a Jew asking the Prophet about the nine signs; its answer continues in the following segment.
rows.anchor: روى عبد الله بن سلمة عن صفوان بن عسال أن يهوديا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report’s answer lists prohibitions against idolatry, theft, adultery, murder, false accusation, sorcery, usury, and fleeing battle, and commands Jews not to violate the Sabbath; the questioner acknowledges prophethood.
rows.anchor: وعليكم خاصة يا يهود أن لا تعتدوا في السبت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to ask Israel may address the Prophet, making proof against them stronger, or a listener, since God has already supplied knowledge.
rows.anchor: هذا أمر للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أن يسأل بني إسرائيل لتكون الحجة عليهم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the command means to inspect what the Qurʾān reports about the Children of Israel.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن معنى السؤال أن تنظر ما في القرآن من أخبار بني إسرائيل عن الحسن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports the variant fa-saʾal as meaning Moses asked Pharaoh to release the Children of Israel.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس أنه قرأ فسأل بني إسرائيل بمعنى فسأل موسى فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s maṣḥūran may mean affected by sorcery, a magician described with a passive form, or deluded by his own magic; Ibn ʿAbbās takes it as deceived.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه إني لأظنك ساحرا فوضع المفعول موضع الفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses says the signs came as proofs that let people see matters of faith and recognize his prophethood; Pharaoh knows they are not magic.
rows.anchor: أي أنزلها حججا وبراهين للناس يبصرون بها أمور دينهم

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī says Pharaoh, God’s enemy, did not know; Moses was the one who said “I know” in the first person.
rows.anchor: وروي أن عليا ع قال في علمت: والله ما علم عدو الله

rows.speaker: قتادة والحسن
rows.claim: Qatāda and al-Ḥasan explain mathbūr as doomed because of disbelief and denial.
rows.anchor: معناه وإني لأعلمك يا فرعون هالكا لكفرك وإنكارك عن قتادة والحسن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it as accursed; Ibn Zayd says irrational, al-Farrāʾ far from good, while the literal reading expresses expectation because destruction depends on persistence.
rows.anchor: وقيل أعلمك ملعونا عن ابن عباس وقيل مخبولا لا عقل لك عن ابن زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh sought to drive Moses and his followers from Egypt and nearby lands, or kill them; God drowned Pharaoh and his whole army while no Israelite perished.
rows.anchor: معناه فأراد فرعون أن يزعج موسى ومن معه من أرض مصر وفلسطين والأردن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Pharaoh’s destruction, Israel is told to dwell in Egypt and Syria; at the final resurrection all are gathered, mixed without tribal separation.
rows.anchor: يعني يوم القيامة عن أكثر المفسرين أي وعد الكرة الآخرة

rows.speaker: الكلبي وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī and Qatāda instead identify the last promise as Jesus’s descent.
rows.anchor: وقيل أراد نزول عيسى عن الكلبي وقتادة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid say lafīfan means everyone together, earliest and latest generations alike.
rows.anchor: وقيل لفيفا أي جميعا أولكم وآخركم عن ابن عباس ومجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān was sent down and descended in truth so people would believe and act on it; it contains and calls to truth.
rows.anchor: أردنا بإنزال القرآن الحق والصواب وهو أن يؤمن به ويعمل بما فيه

rows.speaker: البلخي
rows.claim: Al-Balkhī allows the pronoun to refer to Moses, as in God’s sending down iron, or to the signs, illustrated by Ruʾba’s line.
rows.anchor: وقال البلخي يجوز أن يكون المراد أنزلنا موسى فيكون كقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda cites Ruʾba’s line about black and white streaks and demonstrative wording as a linguistic example for referring to signs collectively.
rows.anchor: فقلت له إن أردت الخطوط فقل كأنها وإن أردت السواد والبياض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet was sent only to announce Paradise to the obedient and warn the disobedient of the Fire.
rows.anchor: مبشرا بالجنة لمن أطاع ومنذرا بالنار لمن عصى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading lightens farraqnāh; ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ubayy, al-Shaʿbī, al-Ḥasan with a variant, Qatāda, and ʿAmr b. Fāʾid use the doubled form, meaning divided into verses and chapters.
rows.anchor: القراءة المشهورة في فرقناه بالتخفيف وروي عن علي ع وابن مسعود

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan explains farraqnāh as separating truth from falsehood; another view divides it into reports, commands, prohibitions, promises, and warnings.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه فرقنا به الحق عن الباطل عن الحسن

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim says God divided the Qurʾān into chapters and verses and revealed it gradually across more than twenty years.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه جعلنا بعضه خبرا وبعضه أمرا وبعضه نهيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gradual revelation lets the Prophet recite steadily, making the text firmer in listeners’ hearts and giving room to reflect; it follows needs and events.
rows.anchor: على تثبت وتؤدة فترتله ليكون أمكن في قلوبهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid explain measured pace as reciting in separate portions rather than rushing.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه لتقرأه عليهم مفرقا شيئا بعد شيء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās prefers slowly reciting Sūrat al-Baqara over reciting the entire Qurʾān quickly.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس أنه قال: لئن أقرأ سورة البقرة وأرتلها أحب إلي

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says not to recite the Qurʾān in fewer than three days and recommends seven.
rows.anchor: وعن عبد الله بن مسعود أنه قال لا تقرأوا القرآن في أقل من ثلاث

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies those given earlier knowledge as people taught the Torah, such as ʿAbd Allāh b. Salām, who knew the Prophet’s description before his mission.
rows.anchor: كعبد الله ابن سلام وغيره فعلموا صفة النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the phrase can include learned people among the People of the Book and others, or Muḥammad’s community.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنهم أهل العلم من أهل الكتاب وغيرهم وقيل إنهم أمة محمد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda say falling on their chins means prostrating on their faces; the chin is named because it is nearest the ground.
rows.anchor: أي يسقطون على الوجوه ساجدين عن ابن عباس وقتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They declare their Lord transcendent above what polytheists attribute to Him and affirm His promise as certainly fulfilled.
rows.anchor: تنزيها لربنا عز اسمه عما يضيف إليه المشركون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They prostrate while weeping from concern over shortcomings in worship, longing for reward, and fear of punishment; Qurʾānic admonition deepens humility, submission, and obedience.
rows.anchor: أي ويسجدون باكين إشفاقا من التقصير في العبادة وشوقا إلى الثواب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the occasion was the Prophet’s nighttime prostration in Mecca, calling God al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm; polytheists mocked that he invoked two gods.
rows.anchor: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كان ساجدا ذات ليلة بمكة يدعو يا رحمن

rows.speaker: ميمون بن مهران
rows.claim: Maymūn b. Mihrān says polytheists objected that they knew al-Raḥīm but not al-Raḥmān.
rows.anchor: أن المشركين قالوا أما الرحيم فنعرفه وأما الرحمن فلا نعرفه

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says Jews objected that the Qurʾān mentions al-Raḥmān less often than the Torah.
rows.anchor: أن اليهود قالوا إن ذكر الرحمن في القرآن قليل وهو في التوراة كثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Any of God’s names may be invoked because all are beautiful; “or” permits either or both names, and mā either reinforces ayyan or means any thing.
rows.anchor: أيا ما تدعوا فله الأسماء الحسنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names of divine essence include Living, Knowing, and Powerful; names for good acts include Creator, Provider, Just, and Merciful; al-Ṣamad describes servants turning to God for needs.
rows.anchor: فأما أسماؤه المنبئة عن صفات ذاته فهو القادر العالم الحي السميع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse establishes one God despite varied names and attributes, recommends invoking beautiful names before petitions, and supports that He does no evil or injustice.
rows.anchor: بين سبحانه في هذه الآية أنه شيء واحد وإن اختلفت أسماؤه وصفاته

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads the command as avoiding public recitation around those who would harm the Prophet, while not suppressing it around those seeking to hear.
rows.anchor: لا تجهر بإشاعة صلاتك عند من يؤذيك ولا تخافت بها عند من يلتمسها منك

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: A report says pagans heard the Prophet’s loud prayer, abused him, and caused harm, so he was told not to recite aloud; this was early in Mecca.
rows.anchor: كان إذا صلى فجهر في صلاته تسمع له المشركون فشتموه وآذوه

rows.speaker: مجاهد وعطاء ومكحول
rows.claim: Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, and Makḥūl, with a similar report from Ibn ʿAbbās, take ṣalāt to mean supplication: neither call loudly nor whisper.
rows.anchor: أن معناه لا تجهر بدعائك ولا تخافت بها ولكن بين ذلك

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim says not to make all prayer loud or quiet: recite night prayers aloud and daytime prayers quietly.
rows.anchor: بأن تجهر بصلاة الليل وتخافت بصلاة النهار عن أبي مسلم

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī says not to recite so loudly as to distract nearby worshippers or so softly that one cannot hear oneself.
rows.anchor: لا تجهر جهرا يشغل به من يصلي بقربك ولا تخافت بها

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: A report from Abū ʿAbd Allāh defines loudness as forceful voice and quietness as inaudibility to one’s own ears, recommending a middle recitation.
rows.anchor: الجهر بها رفع الصوت شديدا والمخافتة ما لم تسمع أذنيك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording says between “that” in the singular because the reference is to the act, as in 2:68.
rows.anchor: ولم يقل بين ذينك لأنه أراد به الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God has no child, which would make Him a created lord rather than Lord of lords; no partner in sovereignty, implying need; and no ally against humiliation, implying weakness.
rows.anchor: أي لم يكن له حليف حالفه لينصره على من يناوئه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid explains God was never humiliated and needs no one to strengthen Him; all worshipped apart from Him are powerless and subdued.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد لم يذل فيحتاج إلى من يتعزز به

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: Muḥammad b. Kaʿb al-Quraẓī says the verse answers Jews and Christians claiming God has a child, Arab polytheists assigning Him a partner, and Sabians and Magians claiming He needs allies.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن في هذه الآية ردا على اليهود والنصارى حين قالوا: اتخذ الله الولد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وسعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Saʿīd b. Jubayr report that the Prophet taught his family this verse and the one before it.
rows.anchor: وروي أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يعلم أهله هذه الآية وما قبلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The praise is not for merely refraining from taking a child or partner; it praises God’s good acts and perfection.
rows.anchor: ليس له الحمد في الآية على أنه لم يفعل وإنما الحمد له سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Bakr through Yaḥyā reads ladunhu with indicated ḍamma on dāl and kasra on hāʾ and nūn; most read ḍamma on dāl and silent nūn. A rare form raises kalimah, read by Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar, al-Ḥasan, Ibn al-Muḥayṣin, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, al-Thaqafī, al-Aʿraj, and ʿAmr b. ʿUbayd.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو بكر برواية يحيى من لدنه بإشمام الدال الضم

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī notes three forms of ladun: with lightened dāl, either deleting its ḍamma or moving it to lām; adjacent consonants explain kasra on nūn, while indicated ḍamma preserves the original vowel.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي في لدن ثلاث لغات لدن مثل سبع ويخفف الدال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min ladunhu may modify shadīd, or may qualify the indefinite noun while containing reference to that noun.
rows.anchor: وأما الجار في قوله من لدنه فيحتمل ضربين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With fatḥa, ʿiwaj is visible physical bending; with kasra it is an abstract flaw in religion or speech. Qayyiman is a circumstantial accusative from anzala.
rows.anchor: العوج بالفتح فيما يرى كالقناة والخشبة وبالكسر فيما لا يرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bākhiʿ means killing or destroying oneself; Dhū al-Rumma’s verse uses it for one consumed by grief over what fate removed.
rows.anchor: والباخع القاتل المهلك يقال بخع نفسه يبخعها بخعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asaf is extreme grief or anger; al-Aʿshā’s verse depicts a man consumed by sorrow.
rows.anchor: والأسف المبالغة في الحزن والغضب يقال أسف فهو آسف وأسيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An lahum ajran is understood as bi-an lahum ajran with the preposition omitted; mākithīn is circumstantial and means abiding.
rows.anchor: تقديره بأن لهم أجرا فحذف الجار

rows.speaker: السراج
rows.claim: Al-Sarrāj analyzes kalimatan as an explanatory accusative like niʿma rajulan Zayd; the first occurrence is omitted and the praised word is implicit because its description follows.
rows.anchor: فقال السراج: انتصب على تفسير المضمر على حد قولهم نعم رجلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis makes kalimatan a transferred specification from the subject, as in sweating blood; the underlying sense is that their utterance was a great word.
rows.anchor: وقيل انتصب كلمة على التمييز المنقول عن الفاعل
